Critics point out that national-level preventive management measures are urgently needed for the elderly as there is a high risk of leading to fatal serious complications such as pneumonia or worsening of underlying diseases in case of infection. According to the Korea Centers for Disease Control and Prevention on the 3rd, the number of people aged 65 or older hospitalized with RSV infection in Korea has continued to increase sharply every year from 433 in 2022 to 1,130 in 2023 and 2032 in 2024. In particular, as of the 3rd of last month (week 40), when the full-fledged epidemic began, the number of patients has already reached 3,300 this year, 1.7 times the total number of patients (1906) last year. The number of patients as well as changes in composition ratio by age are clear. Of the total inpatients (6710) this year, 49.2% of those aged 65 or older accounted for half. Considering that it was only 5.2% in 2022, it shows that the burden of disease from RSV infection has been rapidly shifting from infants to the elderly in recent years. Experts warn that RSV infection in the elderly is at high risk of being directly linked to severe disease. This is because the virus' defense has declined due to immune aging that occurs with age. In addition, lung function and weakened respiratory muscles reduce the ability to spit out airway secretions such as phlegm, making them more vulnerable to infection. According to a study published in the international journal Scientific Report by a team of professors at Korea University Ansan Hospital, 56.8% of RSV hospitalized patients aged 65 or older in Korea were accompanied by pneumonia, and 25% were transferred to intensive care units. Their in-hospital mortality rate reached 10.6%. It is even more fatal for the elderly with underlying diseases. According to an analysis of RSV hospitalized patients aged 60 or older published in the international journal Journal of Infection Digits, 80% of COPD patients, 38% of heart failure patients, and 50% of asthma patients had worsened symptoms of the existing disease during inpatient treatment. In a study of 471 inpatients in the United States, new cardiovascular adverse reactions such as heart failure, atrial fibrillation, and myocardial infarction were identified in 37%. "Korea has limited adult RSV diagnostic tests and relies on a sample monitoring system, so it is easy to underestimate the actual disease burden of high-risk groups," said Park Jin-joo, a professor of circulatory medicine at Seoul National University Bundang Hospital. "We need to upgrade the monitoring system so that we can accurately grasp the overall disease burden and actively inform patients and their guardians of the risk of infection and the need for vaccination." The burden of disease continues for a long time even after acute treatment is over. According to the international academic journal 'Influenza and Arthur's Respiracy Virus', 33% of RSV hospitalized patients aged 60 or older lost their ability to perform daily life such as eating and bathing even six months after discharge, and 38.3% were readmitted within six months. 14% of discharged patients required a higher level of care and care than before admission. RSV, along with flu and COVID-19, is classified as a level 4 legal infectious disease that can be prevented by vaccines. However, the national infectious disease management system still has a wide gap. While the government provides free national vaccination (NIP) for the elderly aged 65 or older in the case of influenza and COVID-19, RSV still focuses only on hygiene management centered on infants and postpartum care centers and childcare facilities. Medical guidelines already specify vaccinations for the elderly. Major domestic and foreign institutions, including the Korean Infectious Society and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), recommend a single dose of RSV vaccine for all adults over the age of 75 and high-risk groups aged 50 to 74 who suffer from chronic diseases or immunocompromised diseases. On the other hand, discussions on introducing domestic NIPs to ensure their access to vaccines have not even taken the first step. RSV infection in the elderly also leads to enormous socioeconomic losses. The international journal 'Journal of Virology' estimated that the total annual medical expenses related to RSV for the elderly exceed 1.48 trillion won. Another academic journal, "Pharmaco Economics Open," also analyzed that an average of 9.37 million won and 10.4 days of hospitalization for RSV infection are required. Experts point out that the burden of such diseases can be substantially relieved through vaccination. According to the international journal "Human Vaccine and ImmunoCeraputics", if people aged 60 or older receive RSV vaccines, direct and indirect costs such as treatment costs and productivity losses are expected to be reduced by a total of 20.675 trillion won. The loss of QALY, an indicator that reflects the deterioration of quality of life due to disease, can also be reduced by 244,424 years. Major overseas countries tend to recognize the cost-effectiveness of vaccines and quickly provide public support. Following the recommendation of vaccination for senior citizens aged 75 to 79, the UK has gradually expanded the scope of support to residents of nursing homes aged 80 or older and those aged 65 to 74 with underlying diseases this year. Australia also provides NIP to those aged 75 or older in consideration of the risk of hospitalization by age, and provides vaccination to indigenous Australians who have a relatively early risk of disease burden from the age of 60. In addition, Canada, Germany, and the United States are continuing to support vaccination for high-risk groups through public health insurance or state programs. Professor Park said, "It is time for Korea to discuss the introduction of NIP by comprehensively evaluating the burden of RSV disease, prevention effect, and cost-effectiveness of vaccines due to aging." content: Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) Nirsevimab is a long-acting monoclonal antibody that provides season-long protection against RSV in infants, reducing medically attended infections and hospitalizations. Maternal vaccination and nirsevimab together offer complementary strategies to protect newborns during their highest-risk months. Year-round access to RSV immunization may reduce major seasonal outbreaks Providing year-round access to RSV immunization would minimize the risk of large seasonal outbreaks across the nation, including in both urban and rural areas. RSV vaccines protect two most-at-risk groups from severe illness The review demonstrates that vaccines for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) are both safe and effective in protecting groups who are most at risk for serious illness, including older adults and infants. RSV vaccine slashes hospitalizations in older adults in real-world trial A large, real-world randomized trial in Denmark found that the RSVpreF vaccine reduced RSV-related hospitalizations in adults aged 60 and over by over 80%. The vaccine also showed protection against broader respiratory illness with a favorable safety profile. Healthy newborns also face high risk of severe RSV infection It is not only premature babies and children with underlying diseases who suffer from serious respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infections. Can an allergy spray help prevent COVID-19? Researchers determine the efficacy and safety of azelastine nasal spray for preventing SARS-CoV-2 infection in healthy adults. How effective is the RSV vaccine for older adults? A single dose of the RSV vaccine offers 58% protection against hospitalization in older adults, but effectiveness varies in immunocompromised individuals. New guidelines improve care for respiratory infections in leukemia patients People with leukemia have a weakened immune system due to the disease itself and treatment, which leads to an increased susceptibility to infections. Maternal RSV vaccination linked to sharp drop in infant lung infections Vaccination of pregnant women has been linked to a drop in newborns being admitted to hospital with a serious lung infection, research suggests. content_title: Subconjunctival Hemorrhage and Respiratory Syncytial Virus Infection in an Infant Evaluated for Non-accidental Trauma: A Case Report of a Possible Association
content: Abstract A six-week-old previously healthy infant was found to have a subconjunctival hemorrhage (SCH) and concomitant respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection. Because SCH in an infant may represent a sentinel finding of non-accidental trauma (NAT), an extensive multidisciplinary evaluation was performed, which identified no traumatic injuries or evidence of abuse. The SCH resolved within one week, and the patient recovered with supportive care without complications. To our knowledge, SCH in association with RSV has not previously been reported, despite RSV being common in infants. As with SCH reported in association with other respiratory infections, inflammatory and pressure-related processes are possible mechanisms, although this observational case cannot establish causation. Reporting this possible association may broaden the differential diagnosis of SCH to include other medical causes in infants with RSV, while reinforcing the need for completing a thorough screening for abuse. Identifying medical causes for childhood injuries is as important as accurately diagnosing inflicted injury, as misdiagnosing child abuse can have serious medicolegal consequences for children and their families. Introduction Subconjunctival hemorrhage (SCH) is a sentinel finding of pediatric non-accidental trauma (NAT), and SCH remains an important and well-documented extraocular manifestation of NAT [1]. However, pediatric SCH has multiple reported age-dependent etiologies such as trauma, Valsalva associated with coughing/vomiting, coagulopathy, and infection, which may overlap with NAT as an etiology. Often, isolated SCH is not fully screened for NAT, and occult injuries are found if there is suspicion for abuse and screening is performed [2]. Ophthalmologists are consulted when there is suspicion of NAT, and full indirect ophthalmoscopic examination through a dilated pupil is recommended for the workup of pediatric/infantile SCH in the setting of suspected NAT [3]. When the NAT workup is normal after identifying only a single sentinel injury, it is prudent to analyze the inciting case findings. This idea is even more important when analyzing a finding like SCH, which has multiple etiologies. To our knowledge, there have been no previous reports of SCH associated with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) identified in searches of PubMed and Google Scholar, although pediatric SCH has rarely been associated with other respiratory infections. This observation is noteworthy, given that RSV is the leading cause of lower respiratory tract infections in children [4]. Herein, we present the case of an infant with SCH in the setting of RSV infection whose comprehensive multidisciplinary NAT evaluation identified no evidence of abuse. The aim is to describe a possible illness-associated explanation of the SCH, as this observational case cannot establish causation or rule out abuse. Case Presentation A six-week-old previously healthy female was admitted to the hospital for increased work of breathing and dehydration. She was evaluated in the emergency department (ED) approximately one week earlier for respiratory symptoms, at which time the initial viral panel was negative, and SCH was not specifically evaluated or documented. Supportive care was provided, and she was discharged with return precautions. On subsequent admission approximately one week later, she tested positive for RSV via polymerase chain reaction testing and was found to have SCH of the right eye (Figure 1). The mother, who accompanied the infant through her evaluations, first noticed the SCH during this hospitalization; she did not report a previous history of ocular or facial trauma. No relevant family history was reported. SCH had not been documented at well-child checks or in birth records. As SCH has been recognized as a sentinel injury in young infants and raises concern for possible abuse, a physical exam and multidisciplinary evaluation were initiated. Initial screening measures included computed tomography (CT) of the head, skeletal survey, and dilated funduscopic examination. Laboratory studies were obtained to evaluate for occult injuries or underlying conditions that would predispose to developing SCH (Table 1). Physical examination revealed no other bruises, abrasions, oral injuries, or deformities. Hemoglobin was 9.5 g/dL, a value which the treating pediatric team considered compatible with the physiologic decline in hemoglobin during early infancy. The red blood cell count of 2.67 x10(6)/mcL and hematocrit of 27.4% were similarly considered age-appropriate. The absolute neutrophil count of 1.01 thou/mcL was also considered within age-appropriate limits. An isolated low anion gap of 1 was obtained from a specimen reported to be mildly hemolyzed, with otherwise reassuring electrolyte findings, and was not considered clinically significant. Platelet count and coagulation studies were within the reported reference ranges. The dilated funduscopic examination was grossly normal, with no retinal hemorrhages noted (Table 2). The head CT demonstrated no acute abnormality (Figure 2A). On the initial skeletal survey, the attending pediatric radiologist noted unilaminar periosteal reaction along the femoral and tibial shafts consistent with normal appositional bone growth for age. However, the radiologist considered the medial left proximal tibial metaphyseal spurring “worthy of further evaluation,” stating that “a transmetaphyseal fracture cannot be excluded on this image and further imaging is warranted” (Figure 2C). The concerning finding was seen on the anteroposterior but not the lateral view and was not a confirmed fracture. Child abuse pediatrics was consulted, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain, spine, and left knee/tibia was obtained. The MRI of the brain (Figure 2B) and spine was reported as normal, and MRI of the left knee/tibia showed no fracture or associated soft tissue injury (Figure 2D). The skeletal studies were interpreted by attending pediatric radiologists, and MRI studies by attending pediatric neuroradiologists. The Department of Children’s Services (DCS) was contacted and evaluated the home and caregivers involved in the infant’s care. The DCS investigation resulted in no concerns. Respiratory treatment was supportive, no intubation was required, and the infant stabilized on room air. The SCH resolved within one week of admission, and no complications or unexpected adverse events were reported. Following the completed medical and psychosocial evaluation, the infant was discharged to the mother with a planned DCS follow-up home visit and repeat skeletal survey after two weeks. At follow-up, no further injuries were identified, and the proximal tibial finding showed no interval change, favoring physiologic periostitis/metaphyseal spurring rather than fracture (Figure 2E). Discussion Trauma is the most common cause of SCH in young children, but SCH has many other non-traumatic causes, including infectious, inflammatory, hematologic, and vascular conditions [1]. In older children, SCH can occur because of indirect vascular trauma secondary to illnesses that increase forceful Valsalva and intrathoracic pressure, including severe coughing, vomiting, constipation, and sneezing. However, these causative mechanisms are not commonly reported in young infants. Koti et al. found SCH to be extremely rare in children under three years old presenting with cough, vomiting, or constipation [5]. Thus, identifying SCH in a young infant should prompt further investigation for physical abuse, particularly because occult injuries may be identified when appropriate screening is performed [2]. Though RSV is one of the leading viral causes of lower respiratory tract illness in infants [4], there is a paucity of information regarding its ocular sequelae. Previous literature has described SCH in association with other infectious illnesses, including herpes zoster [6], varicella [7,8], pertussis [9], Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection [10], and adenovirus-associated respiratory illness [11]. SCH has also been reported in association with COVID-19 and influenza, although these reports are limited and include neonatal and adult patients [12,13]. Despite these reported associations between SCH and other infectious or respiratory illnesses, we identified no previous report specifically describing SCH in association with RSV infection in searches of PubMed and Google Scholar. It is unlikely that the infant reported in this case had a remaining SCH from delivery, as most birth-associated SCH resolve within the first weeks of life [14]. There were also no concerns for constipation, specific coughing events, or other entities that may have caused forceful Valsalva, despite this being an unlikely cause of SCH in this young age group [5]. Furthermore, spontaneous SCH rarely occurs in children, and its presence should prompt an appropriate workup for other medical causes or traumatic injuries [1]. In this patient, the temporal association between SCH and RSV infection, in the absence of another identified medical or traumatic cause after multidisciplinary evaluation, raises the possibility of an illness-related mechanism. One study reported ocular surface inflammation from conditions such as allergic, viral, neonatal, Kawasaki disease, and Herpes Zoster-related conjunctivitis associated with SCH in 13% of children [1]. We hypothesize that the RSV infectious process may contribute to SCH through mechanisms similar to those proposed for other upper respiratory infections such as COVID and influenza: viral remnants in ocular tissues may cause an inflammatory effect that weakens the blood vessels, allowing for an increased propensity for rupture through the increased intrathoracic pressure that accompanies typical sneezing or coughing in many viral upper respiratory infections [12]. Conjunctivitis has been reported in 11% of children hospitalized with RSV [15]. Whether an ocular inflammatory process contributed to the SCH in this infant cannot be established, and no specific coughing or Valsalva event was documented at its onset. Accordingly, these inflammatory and pressure-related pathways remain biologically plausible hypotheses, rather than established mechanisms, in this patient. SCH in the setting of RSV infection may represent a rare illness-associated finding, and recognizing this possibility could be clinically important given the potentially serious medicolegal consequences of both missed abuse and incorrectly attributed abuse. It is also important to state that child abuse cannot be completely excluded simply because imaging, laboratory studies, and physical examination demonstrated no other injuries; however, physicians should consider other non-traumatic causes, though rare, of SCH in infants in the context of a single sentinel injury with a known medical illness that may contribute to a propensity to develop SCH. The importance of maintaining a broad differential diagnosis is supported by a 2026 retrospective cohort study in which Tayama et al. found abuse in only 12 (0.9%) of 1,281 infants and young children with SCH [16]. The Tayama et al. cohort included children aged one to <48 months (mean age 22.5 months); isolated SCH was defined as SCH without another injury identified within seven days before or after the SCH, and abuse ascertainment incorporated diagnosis codes with review of clinical notes and radiology reports. These population-level findings do not remove the need for an age-appropriate abuse evaluation in an individual six-week-old infant. Strengths of this case report include the multidisciplinary evaluation with ophthalmic examination, neuroimaging, skeletal surveys, child abuse pediatrics evaluation, and follow-up imaging. These investigations informed the clinical assessment but cannot definitively exclude abuse or establish RSV causation. Limitations of this case report include the inability to establish the exact timing of SCH onset, although SCH was not documented approximately one week prior to admission during the previous ED visit or at well-child checks or in birth records, the lack of previously reported SCH associated with RSV infections, and the impossibility of entirely ruling out abusive trauma as a cause of SCH, despite multidisciplinary evaluation. Additionally, a single case cannot establish a causal relationship between RSV infection and SCH. Nevertheless, the temporal association between RSV infection and the SCH, analogous reports of SCH in association with other respiratory and infectious illnesses, and the absence of another identified explanation for SCH after multidisciplinary evaluation support consideration of RSV-associated illness as a possible explanation. Further study would be necessary to determine whether SCH represents a reproducible, though rare, ocular finding associated with RSV infection. Conclusions SCH in infants is a sentinel finding of non-accidental trauma, raising the concern for child abuse in specific contexts, and should prompt screening for further injuries. While it is virtually impossible to completely exclude inflicted injury in this case, a multidisciplinary team identified no evidence of abuse or additional traumatic injuries. The temporal association of the SCH with RSV infection indicates the possibility of the RSV infectious process contributing to SCH via inflammatory or pressure-related processes associated with respiratory illness, as has been proposed for other infections. This case documents a possible association, not proof of causation. Nonetheless, considering other medical causes for SCH in infants with RSV, after completing a thorough screening for abuse, is as important as accurately diagnosing inflicted injury given potentially serious medicolegal consequences. content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home Culture – Society Y tế Warning about the burden of respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) on people with chronic diseases. As part of the 2026 Respiratory Syncytial Virus (RSV) Awareness Week (November 2-8), GSK – a multinational biopharmaceutical and healthcare company – announced the results of a global survey on the impact of respiratory syncytial virus on adults with chronic diseases. Find Lung Care Hà Nội Mới•07/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 RSV can affect the health and ability to maintain daily activities in people with chronic illnesses. Photo: Vu Thu The survey, commissioned by GSK and conducted online by Human8 (a global strategic consulting and market research organization), took place from July 15 to August 7, 2026, among 6,041 individuals aged 18 and over in 10 countries, including Australia, Brazil, Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan, Mexico, Poland , Spain, and Taiwan (China). Participants were living with one or more chronic conditions such as cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, type 1 and type 2 diabetes, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and hypertension. Read Med Journals Discover more Check Symptoms Find Treatments Study Biology The survey results showed that up to 79% of participants reported that their daily lives were disrupted when they contracted respiratory infections, including RSV. Infections not only cause physical fatigue but also negatively impact mental health, raising anxiety about managing underlying conditions and forcing patients to become more dependent on family care. Worsening of chronic diseases following respiratory viral infections was observed across several groups: 52% in asthma patients, 45% in COPD patients, 35% in chronic kidney disease patients, 29% in cardiovascular disease patients, and 27% in diabetes patients. Additionally, 36% of participants experienced longer-than-expected recovery times, 25% required follow-up visits to their initial healthcare facility, and 18% needed emergency care. Find Lung Care Notably, in the group previously diagnosed with RSV, symptoms and health effects tend to be more persistent. Approximately 55% of those who had RSV self-reported symptoms as moderate or very severe; this rate rose to 68% in patients with chronic kidney disease or COPD, 64% in those with cardiovascular disease, and 63% in those with asthma. You may also like The 2026 RSV Awareness Week aims to help the community better understand RSV and its impact on adults with chronic diseases. Photo: Vu Thu Following the initial infection, 40% of patients reported continued health problems for a month or more, and nearly 10% needed more than a year to recover or were unable to regain their original health. Globally, RSV is a common respiratory infection, estimated to affect around 64 million people annually across all age groups. Find Lung Care RSV virus is increasingly seen as a dangerous cause of respiratory illness in people aged 60 and older. According to epidemiological studies, in 2019 alone, RSV caused approximately 470,000 hospitalizations and 33,000 in-hospital deaths among the elderly in developed countries. In Vietnam, a five-year forecasting model estimates approximately 4.6 million cases of acute respiratory illness caused by RSV in people aged 60 and over, resulting in around 200,000 hospitalizations and 18,000 deaths related to lower respiratory complications. Although 79% of survey participants expressed concern about respiratory viruses interfering with treatment or worsening underlying conditions, there remains a significant gap in public awareness regarding RSV. Nearly half (46%) of people with chronic illnesses had not discussed RSV with healthcare professionals in the past two years, and 33% of patients had never discussed the virus at all. You may also like In light of this situation, Dr. Elena DeAngelis, Medical Director of GSK Vietnam, emphasized that people with chronic diseases need to proactively monitor their health and discuss directly with healthcare professionals about measures to prevent respiratory viral infections, including RSV. The 2026 RSV Awareness Week aims to promote dialogue between the community and professionals, advising people – especially the elderly and those with underlying health conditions – to proactively seek regular check-ups for scientific advice to protect their respiratory health and maintain a long-term quality of life. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, November 11, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Severe RSV Infections Drive Sharp Short-Term Medical Costs Among Older Japanese Adults by November 10, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Severe RSV Infections Drive Sharp Short-Term Medical Costs Among Older Japanese Adults Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram A retrospective cohort study investigating the health and economic burden of medically attended respiratory syncytial virus infections among older adults across Japan has established that the pathogen precipitates substantial, statistically significant short-term increases in healthcare resource utilization and medical expenditures. Drawing information across an observation window spanning 1 September 2008 through 31 August 2021, investigators evaluated records from two prominent administrative repositories: the hospital-based Medical Data Vision claims database and the employer-based JMDC claims database. The research team identified 178 confirmed index events occurring in patients aged 60 years and older between 2009 and 2019, comprising 144 individuals drawn from the hospital-centered Medical Data Vision records and 34 individuals identified within the employment-affiliated JMDC dataset. Across these cohorts, older adults diagnosed with respiratory syncytial virus experienced extensive clinical complications alongside acute escalations in outpatient consultations and hospital admissions, culminating in substantial financial consequences during the initial month following diagnosis that were primarily driven by inpatient hospitalization costs. Respiratory syncytial virus has long been recognized as a leading cause of acute respiratory illness in vulnerable populations, including young pediatric patients and aging adults. In older individuals, particularly those presenting with preexisting cardiovascular diseases, pulmonary conditions, or metabolic disorders like diabetes, infection can progress toward life-threatening manifestations such as severe pneumonia or lower respiratory tract disease, frequently demanding urgent hospitalization or non-invasive mechanical ventilation. Beyond acute primary damage, viral replication can stimulate inflammatory cascades that trigger critical exacerbations of underlying chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, bronchial asthma, and congestive heart failure. Despite these established clinical trajectories, the true epidemiology and financial consequences of respiratory syncytial virus among older demographics in Japan have historically remained underreported. Discover more Biotech startup funding Learn Engineering Track Biotech To rigorously delineate these disease patterns, the researchers examined multi-year datasets capturing inpatient and outpatient health claims across acute-care and commercial insurance networks. The Medical Data Vision repository incorporates anonymized Japanese Diagnosis Procedure Combination records detailing acute-care hospital inpatient care and lump-sum payment systems, containing approximately 45 million patient profiles of which roughly 35 percent represent individuals aged over 65 years. Complementing this acute inpatient framework, the JMDC database compiles health insurance claims from more than 130 payer organizations, encapsulating inpatient admissions, ambulatory encounters, prescription dispensing services, and regular health checkup evaluations across 12 million insured lives, where approximately 2 percent represent adults aged 65 to 74 years. The study protocol mapped distinct twelve-month annual identification cycles running from September through August between 2009 and 2020. This longitudinal architecture required a baseline observation window spanning 365 days prior to the first confirmed diagnostic claim alongside a structured follow-up monitoring period after the index viral infection. Discover more Engineering job board Research publication platform Scientific instrument sales Laboratory equipment supplier Case qualification required patients aged 60 years or older to demonstrate at least one documented medical claim carrying a specific Tenth Revision International Statistical Classification of Diseases code indicative of respiratory syncytial virus infection, encompassing diagnostic classifications B34.8, J12.1, J20.5, or J21.0. Because administrative datasets lack explicit laboratory confirmation dates, index diagnosis dates were established through systematic database-specific algorithms integrating treatment initiation markers, hospital admission records, service delivery timelines, and monthly claims submissions. Within the Medical Data Vision cohort, the mean patient age was 74.5 years with a standard deviation of 9.1 years, and 58 percent of these individuals received medical management in tertiary medical centers containing more than 500 beds. Within the JMDC cohort, which was restricted by database coverage to individuals aged 60 to 74 years, the mean age stood at 64.0 years with a standard deviation of 3.6 years, and 47 percent were evaluated within smaller medical clinics maintaining fewer than 20 beds. Across the entire 2009 through 2019 timeline, the overall documented incidence rate within the Medical Data Vision cohort was calculated at 0.007 per 1,000 person-years. Preexisting medical comorbidities were documented during the 365-day baseline window, revealing that 93 to 94 percent of patients presented with chronic underlying disorders prior to acquiring their viral infection. The overall burden of baseline illness differed markedly between the study populations, reflecting the distinct structural characteristics of each database. The median modified Charlson comorbidity index reached 5 in the hospital-based Medical Data Vision cohort compared to 1 in the younger, employment-based JMDC population. The most prevalent baseline comorbidities recorded across the study cohorts included type 2 diabetes, congestive heart failure, systemic hypertension, solid malignant tumors, chronic liver failure, bronchial asthma, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Every identified patient demonstrated concurrent manifestations of lower respiratory tract disease, upper respiratory tract disease, or both during their primary episode. Lower respiratory tract conditions were identified in 78.5 percent of Medical Data Vision patients and 58.8 percent of JMDC patients, confirming that medically attended presentations in older Japanese adults predominantly involve deep pulmonary pathology. Acute clinical complications arising between seven days prior to the index diagnosis date and fourteen days following diagnosis were exceptionally frequent, occurring in 61.1 percent of the Medical Data Vision cohort and 55.9 percent of the JMDC cohort. Documented secondary clinical events included acute congestive heart failure decompensation, bacterial and viral pneumonia, acute bronchitis, and acute respiratory failure. Among individuals possessing a documented baseline history of bronchial asthma, acute disease exacerbations occurred in 25.0 percent of the Medical Data Vision group and 20.0 percent of the JMDC group. Furthermore, among Medical Data Vision patients with preexisting chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, 18.8 percent suffered acute pulmonary exacerbations during their infection, whereas no such exacerbations were cataloged within the smaller JMDC cohort. Therapeutic interventions reflected this clinical severity, with diagnostic chest radiography and therapeutic oxygen inhalation emerging as the two most frequently administered procedures, both displaying statistically significant post-diagnosis utilization increases across all evaluated intervals. Evaluation of healthcare resource utilization demonstrated marked, statistically significant increases when comparing the acute 30-day post-diagnosis window against the average 30-day baseline consumption derived across the preceding pre-event year. Within the Medical Data Vision cohort, the average number of outpatient consultations per patient rose from a baseline mean of 1.21 visits to 2.07 visits in the post-event timeframe, representing a statistically significant escalation supported by paired sample testing. Concurrently, the average frequency of inpatient hospitalizations increased more than fivefold, rising from a baseline mean of 0.07 admissions per individual to 0.37 admissions during the acute month following diagnosis. Similar patterns appeared in the JMDC cohort, where outpatient encounters exhibited an average increase of 1.44 visits per patient, moving from 2.15 baseline visits to 3.59 visits during the acute post-event interval. These spikes in hospitalizations and outpatient attendances subsided across subsequent observation windows of 180 and 365 days, indicating that acute healthcare operational pressures normalize toward baseline values once the acute viral infection resolves. The economic burden accompanying these heightened medical interventions was substantial, with the Medical Data Vision cohort demonstrating a statistically significant average cost increase of 196,231.7 Japanese yen per patient during the initial 30 days post-diagnosis. Mean healthcare spending surged from a 30-day pre-event baseline of 132,109.7 yen to 328,341.4 yen post-diagnosis. Inpatient hospital admissions served as the dominant economic driver, contributing an additional 187,256.0 yen in hospital lodging and acute therapeutic fees as inpatient costs expanded from 89,544.9 yen to 276,800.9 yen. Subgroup stratification illustrated that financial consequences scaled directly with advancing patient age. Individuals aged 60 to 74 years incurred an average cost rise of 122,552.2 yen, whereas patients aged 75 years and older experienced an average expenditure surge of 280,908.1 yen, of which 270,903.9 yen stemmed entirely from inpatient hospitalization expenses. Clinical stratification further revealed that patients presenting with lower respiratory tract disease experienced a mean cost surge of 234,250.6 yen driven by hospital admissions, while patients exhibiting isolated upper respiratory tract involvement experienced a non-significant cost change of 57,646.7 yen. Preexisting medical vulnerability heavily influenced incremental expenditure profiles across comorbidity subgroups within the hospital-based population. Similarly, patients diagnosed with baseline cardiovascular disorders recorded an overall expenditure increase of 267,994.7 yen, predominantly governed by a 264,880.7 yen expansion in hospital inpatient care. Subgroups with diagnosed type 2 diabetes and chronic pulmonary conditions generated incremental cost burdens of 175,618.8 yen and 150,362.9 yen, respectively, with inpatient diabetes admissions accounting for 171,005.5 yen of that group’s expenditure surge. Hospitalization frequencies expanded across all comorbidity cohorts, increasing by an average of 0.39 admissions per patient among cardiovascular cases, 0.30 among diabetic cases, 0.28 among renal failure cases, and 0.26 among patients with chronic pulmonary disease, confirming that underlying organ dysfunction amplifies inpatient admission risks during acute infection. The study authors highlighted several methodological considerations that contextualize their findings and delineate clear boundaries for clinical interpretation. Because the Medical Data Vision dataset exclusively captures hospital-based claims, it inherently samples an older population displaying heightened clinical acuity, meaning that observed utilization rates and monetary costs cannot be generalized directly to mild or unmanaged community infections. Furthermore, the mandatory requirement that Medical Data Vision participants maintain continuous claims every six months across baseline and follow-up intervals may have excluded individuals with milder illness who did not seek routine healthcare, potentially overestimating per-patient burden while underestimating overall population infection volumes. Administrative coding limitations, reliance on indirect diagnostic estimation algorithms rather than exact clinical testing timestamps, single-event indexing per annual cycle, and potential coding overlap across nonspecific lower respiratory categories also represent analytical constraints. Nevertheless, by demonstrating significant short-term cost spikes and severe acute complications among hospitalized older adults, these real-world findings provide critical baseline evidence to inform future clinical management, diagnostic vigilance, and targeted vaccination initiatives across Japan. Relief for Parents During RSV Season more/close Fred Hutch researchers confirm that infant anti-RSV therapies remain highly effective and create an early-warning system to detect viral changes that could undermine their protection November 10, 2026 • By John Higgins / Fred Hutch News Service Video by Robert Hood / Fred Hutch News Service The first thing Cassandra Simonich, MD, PhD, wants parents to know about protecting their infants during cold and flu season is that the current prevention therapies for respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, are safe, effective and recommended. But Simonich, a research associate at Fred Hutch Cancer Center and a pediatric infectious diseases physician at Seattle Children’s, also knows that viruses change over time and therapies that are highly effective today might be less so if the virus evolves resistance. To improve how researchers monitor changes in RSV, she collaborated with Jesse Bloom, PhD, an evolutionary virologist at Fred Hutch. They recently published the results of that collaboration in the journal Nature. The study applied a technique developed in the Bloom Lab to safely investigate all the potential ways that RSV could evolve to resist these therapies. Subscribe to Fred Hutch News You will receive a free monthly newsletter from us about our innovative research and compassionate care as well as updates on events and other helpful tools and tips. You may unsubscribe at any time. Listen to the audio interview Libsyn | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Amazon Podcasts | YouTube The team analyzed more than 60,000 genomic sequences of the virus from all over the world sampled from people with RSV and published in public databases. Their investigation confirmed that resistance to current therapies has arisen sporadically but remains rare. The team also discovered a weak link that explains why one of the two major subtypes of RSV is more susceptible to resistance mutations than the other. Their innovative approach enables real-time surveillance for natural RSV strains with resistance mutations and provides a road map to weak links in RSV and potentially in other viruses that researchers can use to make better therapies. Current therapies work, which requires vigilance to keep it that way RSV is one of many viruses that causes the common cold in healthy adults but poses a greater threat to infants, older adults with weakened immune systems and people who are immunocompromised – such as when undergoing cancer treatment. The virus remains the leading cause of infant hospitalization in the United States. Though it’s seldom fatal in the U.S. and other countries with advanced health care systems, it’s a leading cause of infant mortality globally, especially in less developed countries. RSV vaccines are available for vulnerable adults, and a vaccinated mother can pass protective antibodies to her infant, but that approach only works in a narrow window of time. The maternal RSV vaccine (Pfizer's Abrysvo) is given during weeks 32-36 of pregnancy, and maternal antibodies protect the baby against RSV for approximately six months after birth, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. There is no RSV vaccine for infants, but they can receive RSV immunization with ready-made antibodies that provide immediate protection and last at least five months to see infants through the RSV season. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends RSV immunization for all infants under 8 months of age born during or entering their first RSV season unless they are protected by a maternal vaccination during pregnancy. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends either nirsevimab or clesrovimab for all babies younger than 8 months born to mothers who didn’t receive a maternal RSV vaccine during pregnancy. “It's so incredible — as a physician, as a pediatrician, and as a mom — that we now can use these things to prevent RSV disease,” Simonich said. “We know that these things are highly effective. They work really well.” For example, the most widely used RSV antibody, nirsevimab, has demonstrated roughly 75% to 80% effectiveness against RSV-associated hospitalizations of infants and (along with maternal vaccination) has reduced infant hospitalizations in countries where it is widely used, according to the Nature study. But viruses can evolve to escape such antibodies. One RSV antibody failed clinical trials because of a resistant strain, and resistance mutations have popped up sporadically to nirsevimab. “Fortunately, it's rare, but we need to be on the lookout,” Simonich said. “The field has been really diligent, and they've been really focused on monitoring RSV very closely for any signs of resistance.” But the standard methods for keeping tabs on the evolution of the virus are slow and labor intensive, which is why Simonich turned to the Bloom Lab at Fred Hutch to try a new approach. A safe way to build an early-warning system Typically, researchers have found resistance mutations either by watching the virus evolve in laboratory experiments or by analyzing virus samples from patients one at a time. “The monitoring up to this point had been kind of limited because basically there wasn't a thorough or comprehensive understanding of the impact of any viral changes that they observed without monitoring what they actually mean for the ability of these antibodies to still effectively target the virus,” Simonich said. Over the last few years, Bloom’s team in the Basic Sciences Division has figured out a new way to get that big picture quickly by safely running thousands of experiments simultaneously to discover which possible mutations matter for virus survival and should raise an alarm if they pop up on the radar of surveillance efforts. They call the method pseudovirus-based deep mutational scanning, which involves genetically engineering a pseudovirus that can infect a cell like the real thing, but only once. The pseudovirus cannot reproduce and spread like an actual virus, making it much safer for experimentation. They also add some features to the pseudovirus to streamline its use for deep mutational scanning experiments that can systematically measure the effects of thousands of mutations on a virus’ ability to infect cells and escape virus-killing antibodies. The Bloom Lab has used the method to identify mutations to the infamous “spike” protein in the virus that causes COVID-19, which have helped the virus dodge our vaccines and outrun our growing natural immunity. The lab has also used the method to safely investigate the much rarer but more deadly Nipah virus. Working with Simonich, the lab analyzed 60,000 RSV sequences from public databases to test the effects of potential mutations to a critical molecular complex called a fusion protein, which allows the virus to glom onto a cell. The anti-RSV antibodies work because they bind to the fusion protein and prevent it from fusing the membranes of the virus and the host cell. When it’s locked and blocked by the antibodies, the fusion protein can’t enter the host cell to infect it. But resistance mutations to the fusion protein might interfere with the locking and blocking, which would make what is now an effective therapy less effective. “The really nice thing about this system is that we don't ever have to use any actual RSV virus,” Simonich said. “We just use a little piece and focus on the target of the antibody, which is the fusion protein. And so that makes it a really, really safe way to generate these comprehensive maps.” The team used the system to measure the effect of every possible mutation on antibody effectiveness. Simonich estimated that less than 1% of RSV sequences contain resistance mutations. “When we scored all of these sequences, we find that strains with resistance mutations are exceedingly rare,” she said. They integrated their scoring system into Nextstrain — an open-access platform for monitoring pathogens — to create a real-time early warning system so researchers can be on the lookout for the mutations most likely to cause trouble. The analysis confirmed that the current RSV immunization therapies are working as intended. But when they dug deeper into the data and performed some additional experiments, they discovered a weak link in the system that RSV could exploit to evade those therapies. Experiments reveal a weak link that viruses could exploit The viral sequences the team analyzed included two main subtypes — RSV A and RSV B — which circulate together. The subtypes are similar in almost every way, but while resistant mutations are rare overall, they are more common in subtype B than subtype A. Nobody knew why. “That was really confusing to the field because if you look sort of generally, nirsevimab seems to neutralize both subtypes very similarly,” Simonich said. “They really are similar in terms of their sequence. They're similar in their structure. It was a really big question, so we really dug into this.” The nirsevimab antibodies have two hands that both grab the fusion protein to lock and block it, but the team discovered that the hands get a tighter grip on subtype A than they do on subtype B. Certain mutations weaken the grip of nirsevimab on both subtypes, but the effect isn’t the same because the starting grip strength is stronger on subtype A than it is…

Shop Donate November 10, 2026 RSV season has started. Who can get the vaccine? Infectious Diseases Vaccines Sandy Laping, MSc and Heather Duncan, MPH, PhD RSV immunization is recommended for babies, some toddlers, pregnant people, and many older adults. With fall in full swing, winter respiratory virus season is also getting into gear and, like every year, it brings along infectious diseases like COVID, flu, and RSV. A quick refresher – what is RSV? RSV stands for Respiratory Syncytial Virus, or RSV for short (it’s pronounced RES-pih-ruh-TOR-ee sin-SIH-shul VY-rus ). It’s a very common virus that affects the upper respiratory system and the lungs, and most people catch it as babies or toddlers. It’s the most common cause of bronchiolitis (an inflammation of the small airways in the lungs) and pneumonia in kids under 1 year, and the most common cause for hospitalization in that age group. In healthy folks, it usually feels like a cold, but it can be serious in older adults and people who have a weakened immune system, are frail, and those with certain medical conditions that affect the heart and lungs. RSV spreads through coughs and sneezes, through droplets, and also through contact with surfaces that are contaminated with RSV particles (we call this fomite transmission). The main season for RSV tends to be from fall into winter and through to early spring, but does depend on geographical location. Now to the good news! Immunization is available for older adults and babies, and the evidence shows that these are great at preventing severe disease and hospitalizations. So who can get an RSV vaccine? There are several FDA-approved RSV vaccine products for adults 60 and older as well as adults ages 18 to 59 who have a higher risk of severe infection. One RSV vaccine is also approved during pregnancy (32-36 weeks), which helps protect the baby during infancy. And for infants born without this protection, there are monoclonal antibody shots that can prevent RSV. Some children under two need another shot during their second RSV season if they have risks for severe infection. The American Medical Association (AMA), in collaboration with some other organizations, compiled a list of recommendations that are based on a recent independent review of the evidence of the available immunizations. Here are their recommendations: Children 0-18 years: Babies under 8 months old should get an RSV immunization before entering their first cold and flu season. This is unless their birth parent was vaccinated during pregnancy. Children between 8 and 19 months old who are at high risk of severe RSV disease and are entering their second RSV season should also be immunized. No RSV immunizations are currently approved for people 2 to 17 years of age. Parents and caregivers of immunocompromised children and teens in this age group can talk with their clinician about other ways to lower their RSV risk. Pregnant folks: If the pregnant person is between 32 and 36 weeks of pregnancy between Sept. 1st and March 1st, they should receive an RSV vaccine during that time period unless they have a planned delivery within the following two weeks, have already received the maternal RSV vaccine during a previous pregnancy, or are planning to have their baby receive a monoclonal antibody (nirsevimab or clesrovimab, which offer temporary protection from RSV) after birth. Adults 19-64: Healthy adults between the ages of 19 and 49 are not recommended to receive the RSV vaccine. However, if you are 50 or older and at increased risk for severe RSV, you should receive a vaccine. Older Adults aged 65+: Adults between 65 and 74 who are at increased risk of severe RSV should be vaccinated. All adults (regardless of risk) 75 and older should receive the vaccine. Immunocompromised folks: All people aged 18 or older who are immunocompromised should receive the RSV vaccine. Healthcare workers: There is no special guidance for clinicians working in the healthcare field. These folks should follow the age- and risk-based recommendations for the vaccine. Is it covered by insurance? As is usually the case, it depends. If you purchased an insurance plan through your state’s health insurance marketplace and you meet the CDC clinical recommendations for immunization, then your RSV vaccine will be covered. Most private insurance plans, such as one you receive through your employer, will also cover RSV vaccination if it is clinically indicated. If you are on Medicaid, your RSV vaccine will be covered as long as you are in a group recommended to receive it, along with any other vaccine that is recommended by ACIP (Advisory Committee for Immunization Practices). Although ACIP has not met since December 2025, health insurers who are part of the trade organization AHIP(America’s Health Insurance Plans), and both Medicaid and Medicare continue to cover the cost of most vaccinations for now, provided you are eligible. Infants are eligible for the vaccine and monoclonal antibodies under CHIP and the Vaccines for Children program. Pregnant folks on Medicaid will have their maternal vaccine covered. If you are on Medicare and you have Part D or a Medicare Advantage Plan, your vaccine will be covered. If not, you will have to pay out of pocket for the vaccine. And remember, all the usual ways to protect yourself and those around you from catching any winter germs also help: these include staying home when sick, testing when unwell, strategic masking, and handwashing. content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Wednesday, November 11, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Hospitalized Adults With Rhinovirus Face Severe In-Hospital Outcomes Similar to RSV by November 10, 2026 in Biology, Health Reading Time: 6 mins read 0 Hospitalized Adults With Rhinovirus Face Severe In-Hospital Outcomes Similar to RSV Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Hospitalized adult patients infected with rhinovirus experience severe in-hospital clinical outcomes at rates comparable to those infected with respiratory syncytial virus, according to a retrospective observational cohort study conducted in southern Brazil. Published in Discover Viruses, the investigation tracked adult inpatients admitted to Moinhos de Vento Hospital in Porto Alegre between April 2022 and July 2023, a period defined by the dominance of the SARS-CoV-2 Omicron variant and the conclusion of the national COVID-19 epidemic emergency. The primary composite outcome—consisting of in-hospital death, the requirement for invasive mechanical ventilation, and admission to an intensive care unit—occurred in more than one-third of the analyzed individuals across both viral cohorts. By demonstrating that patients suffering from rhinovirus infections faced clinical trajectories characterized by high rates of critical care intervention and death that were statistically indistinguishable from those observed in respiratory syncytial virus cases, the researchers challenge long-standing clinical assumptions that classify rhinoviruses merely as mild, low-virulence upper respiratory pathogens among hospitalized adults. The clinical motivation for comparing these two common respiratory pathogens stems from the substantial global healthcare burden imposed by acute respiratory viral infections. Globally, these infections are responsible for an estimated 24.80 cases per 10,000 adults and contribute to roughly six percent of worldwide mortality and disability, while also being implicated in 25 to 60 percent of community-acquired pneumonia presentations. Historically, infectious disease frameworks have categorized rhinoviruses as agents of low virulence that typically cause benign, self-limiting colds, whereas respiratory syncytial virus has consistently been recognized as a high-virulence pathogen capable of causing devastating lower respiratory tract disease, particularly among newborns, young children, and elderly individuals. However, during the Omicron phase and the broader post-pandemic transition, both viruses re-emerged as leading causes of severe adult respiratory hospitalizations. Despite this shared clinical prominence, few investigations have directly evaluated in-hospital outcomes between hospitalized adults infected with rhinovirus and those infected with respiratory syncytial virus. Discover more Biotech startup funding Learn Engineering Track Biotech To address this knowledge gap, the research team implemented an observational retrospective cohort design at Moinhos de Vento Hospital, a tertiary private teaching medical center situated in Porto Alegre, Brazil. The metropolitan context surrounding the hospital encompasses approximately 4.5 million residents, with 1.5 million living directly within the city of Porto Alegre. The cohort included hospitalized patients aged 14 years and older who underwent molecular virological testing and received a confirmed positive result for either rhinovirus or respiratory syncytial virus between April 2022 and July 2023. This age threshold of 14 years was selected because the institution’s administrative Diagnosis Related Group database categorizes individuals above this threshold as adult patients. The investigation deliberately excluded pregnant women, newborns, and pediatric patients under the age of 14. Enrolled participants received clinical care and diagnostic testing across multiple hospital locations, including general inpatient medical wards, the emergency department, and intensive care units, and the overall study adhered strictly to the STROBE reporting guidelines. Discover more Engineering job board Research publication platform Scientific instrument sales Laboratory equipment supplier The virological diagnosis of enrolled patients relied on advanced molecular techniques that were implemented alongside the hospital’s introduction of an expanded respiratory panel capable of detecting 24 different viral and bacterial pathogens. Biological samples were obtained through nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal swabs utilizing standardized Kolplast collection kits manufactured in Itupeva, São Paulo, Brazil, or collected via bronchoalveolar lavage when clinically indicated. The harvested specimens were processed at the hospital’s dedicated Genetics and Molecular Biology Laboratory, where viral genetic material was extracted using the MagMAX Viral and Pathogen Binding Beads kit produced by Thermo Fisher. Following extraction, multiplex polymerase chain reaction amplification was carried out, followed by reverse hybridization dot-blot assays with pathogen-specific probes fixed onto nylon membranes using Flow-Chip Technology on automated HybriSpot12Auto equipment from the Vitro Group. This diagnostic platform specifically identified rhinovirus and both subtypes A and B of respiratory syncytial virus, resolving any rare co-detections by sorting the primary exposure according to the initial detected pathogen. Patient laboratory records were linked through deterministic matching algorithms to the hospital’s Diagnosis Related Group administrative database to assemble detailed clinical profiles, comorbidity measures, and acute hospitalization trajectories. The Diagnosis Related Group classification represents an established administrative and billing system that groups patients sharing comparable clinical conditions, baseline comorbidity burdens, and resource consumption patterns. By analyzing primary and secondary diagnostic codes from the International Classification of Diseases alongside procedures performed during admission and demographic characteristics, the system generates an objective case mix index reflecting overall patient complexity. The primary outcome was designated as a composite measure encompassing in-hospital mortality, the need for mechanical ventilation, and intensive care unit admission. Secondary endpoints comprised each individual component of the composite measure, the overall hospital length of stay, and the number of days alive and out of the hospital calculated across a 30-day window from the initial day of hospital admission. The metric of days alive and out of the hospital was evaluated over a 30-day timeframe to mitigate the confounding effect that in-hospital mortality exerts on conventional measures of hospitalization length of stay. For this calculation, researchers subtracted the total number of days spent hospitalized from 30, assigning a value of zero days to any patient who died prior to discharge, though post-discharge deaths could not be captured. In their statistical analysis, the authors employed Student’s t-tests or Mann-Whitney tests for continuous variables and Chi-square tests for categorical distributions. To assess the independent association between the infecting viral pathogen and the composite primary outcome, a multivariable logistic regression model was fitted, adjusting for patient sex, chronological age, and the baseline Diagnosis Related Group case mix index. Furthermore, hospital length of stay and days alive and out of the hospital were analyzed under discrete count assumptions using Poisson regression with correction for overdispersion, adjusting for identical demographic and clinical covariates in Jamovi and R software. During the fifteen-month study window, hospital clinicians performed 3,329 molecular tests for suspected acute respiratory viral infections, identifying 329 positive results for the examined viruses, comprising 216 patients with rhinovirus and 113 with respiratory syncytial virus. Baseline demographic comparisons revealed that patients in the respiratory syncytial virus cohort were significantly older than their counterparts in the rhinovirus group, presenting a mean age of 69.72 years with a standard deviation of 21.24, compared to a mean age of 64.10 years with a standard deviation of 22.98 among those with rhinovirus, producing a statistically significant p-value of 0.03. In contrast, gender distributions between the two viral groups showed no significant difference, with males accounting for 49.07 percent of rhinovirus cases and 45.13 percent of respiratory syncytial virus cases. Similarly, the underlying comorbidity burden was well balanced, as reflected by median case mix scores of 0.93 with an interquartile range of 0.76 to 1.65 for rhinovirus and 1.15 with an interquartile range of 0.92 to 1.75 for respiratory syncytial virus. When evaluating the occurrence of acute clinical deterioration, the researchers discovered that the primary composite outcome occurred in 33.80 percent of patients with rhinovirus infections and 37.17 percent of patients diagnosed with respiratory syncytial virus. Multivariable logistic regression adjusting for age, sex, and the Diagnosis Related Group case mix score yielded an adjusted odds ratio of 1.02 with a 95 percent confidence interval spanning from 0.59 to 1.78 and a p-value of 0.94, confirming no statistically significant difference in composite risk. Examination of individual components also revealed comparable severity profiles between the two pathogens. Intensive care unit admission was required for 31.94 percent of the rhinovirus cohort and 34.51 percent of the respiratory syncytial virus cohort, with a non-significant p-value of 0.63. Mechanical ventilation was administered to 12.96 percent of rhinovirus patients and 9.73 percent of respiratory syncytial virus patients, with a p-value of 0.39, while in-hospital mortality reached 9.26 percent in the rhinovirus cohort compared to 7.96 percent in the respiratory syncytial virus group, yielding a p-value of 0.69. Hospital utilization metrics further confirmed that patients hospitalized with rhinovirus required medical resources on a scale comparable to those infected with respiratory syncytial virus. The median length of hospital stay stood at 9.60 days with an interquartile range of 5.67 to 17.20 days in the rhinovirus group, compared to a median of 9.20 days with an interquartile range of 5.20 to 15.20 days among individuals infected with respiratory syncytial virus, yielding a p-value of 0.62. In the adjusted Poisson regression model, the odds ratio for length of stay was 0.96 with a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.78 to 1.17 and a p-value of 0.67. Similarly, the mean number of days alive and out of the hospital over the 30-day evaluation period was 20.20 days for rhinovirus and 20.10 days for respiratory syncytial virus, reflecting an adjusted odds ratio of 1.10 with a 95 percent confidence interval of 0.98 to 1.24 and a p-value of 0.12. Violin plot representations of these distributions documented equivalent duration patterns, after excluding two extreme outlier lengths of stay of 235 and 236 days from the respiratory syncytial virus visualization. The study authors highlighted several methodological limitations that provide essential context for interpreting these clinical observations. A post-hoc analysis revealed a viral co-infection rate of 4.86 percent across the sample, with 1.86 percent of patients co-infected with both rhinovirus and respiratory syncytial virus, all of whom were older than 90 years. Additionally, the retrospective design could not distinguish whether the detected viral infection was the primary precipitating cause of admission or an incidental finding, although prior literature indicates low rates of hospital-acquired respiratory infections. Furthermore, the administrative case mix index may not fully reflect disease lethality compared to resource consumption, and the focus on hospitalized adults in a private tertiary center prevents generalization to broader community populations. Testing was also subject to selection bias, as clinicians may have prioritized testing for patients presenting with heightened baseline illness severity, potentially inflating observed mortality and mechanical ventilation rates. Tiago Finger Andreis at Moinhos de Vento Hospital maintains the underlying datasets, which remain accessible upon reasonable institutional request. Subject of Research: In-hospital outcomes and clinical severity of rhinovirus compared to respiratory syncytial virus infections in hospitalized adult patients. Article Title: In-hospital outcomes of rhinovirus and respiratory syncytial virus infections: a retrospective cohort study Article References: dos Santos Hoffmann, E., Decker, S. R. D. content_title: Mechanical Ventilation and Vasopressor Use Flag RSV Deaths
content: Jump to Key Points The use of mechanical ventilation and vasopressors was the most significant factor associated with 30-day mortality among adults hospitalized with respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection, based on data from 209 individuals presented at the Infectious Disease Week (IDWeek) 2026 Annual Meeting. “Although respiratory syncytial virus has traditionally been associated with pediatric respiratory infections , it is now recognized as a significant cause of severe respiratory illness in adults, particularly those with comorbidities,” said lead author Eduardo Becerril-Vargas, PhD, of the Instituto Nacional de Enfermedades Respiratorias, Mexico City, Mexico. The researchers sought to identify clinical characteristics associated with 30-day mortality to identify patients at higher risk for complications, he said. “One of the most significant findings was the extent of severe disease: 24 of the 209 patients (11.5%) died within the first 30 days, and 18.7% required invasive mechanical ventilation,” Becerril-Vargas emphasized. The study population included 209 adults aged 46-71 years who were hospitalized with RSV; the median age was 59 years, 51% of the patients were female, and 91% had at least one comorbidity. SUGGESTED FOR YOU Approximately one third (33.5%) of the patients had coinfections, most of which were bacterial, said Becerril-Vargas. “Although bacterial coinfection was associated with higher mortality in the unadjusted analysis, the primary factors associated with mortality in the multivariable analysis were mechanical ventilation, prolonged use of vasopressors, and a higher burden of comorbidities,” he said. “These findings show that the severity of RSV in hospitalized adults is related both to the patient’s clinical condition and to complications that develop during hospitalization,” he noted. The most common radiologic findings associated with 30-day mortality were interstitial infiltrates on chest x-rays and ground-glass opacity on CT, present in 13.8% and 23.9% of the study population, respectively. In addition, laboratory data showed higher creatinine and C-reactive protein levels and lower albumin levels in the 24 patients who died within 30 days than in those who survived. Limitations and Next Steps The study had several limitations, including the retrospective design and the use of data from a single center specializing in respiratory diseases; consequently, the patients may have more complex conditions than those treated in general hospitals, said Becerril-Vargas. “Furthermore, the number of deaths was relatively limited, a fact that should be taken into account when interpreting the estimates from the multivariable analysis. As this is an observational study, the associations identified do not establish causality,” he said. “However, the study supports the recognition of RSV as a significant cause of severe respiratory illness in adults rather than exclusively as a pediatric infection,” he added. “Our findings underscore the importance of timely virologic diagnosis, the assessment of comorbidities, and the early identification of respiratory and hemodynamic deterioration,” said Becerril-Vargas. “In patients with severe disease, it is also important to investigate potential bacterial coinfections and to guide antimicrobial treatment based on clinical and microbiological findings,” he added. Prospective, multicenter studies are needed in populations with varying levels of disease severity in order to validate these prognostic factors and to evaluate the impact of prevention, vaccination, and clinical care strategies on mortality, Becerril-Vargas said. Filling a Knowledge Gap The current study adds to the limited amount of data on RSV in older adults compared to the data available for children, said Anastasia Wasylyshyn, MD, clinical assistant professor of infectious disease at the University of Michigan Medical School in Ann Arbor. “Trying to determine who is most likely to have severe outcomes is a useful undertaking, so that vaccine or other preventative therapies could be better directed in the future,” said Wasylyshyn, who was not involved in the study. The finding of higher mortality rates in adults with more severe critical illness was not unexpected, but the data highlight the severity of illness as independent of other risk factors associated with mortality in this population, Wasylyshyn noted. Looking ahead, reexamining the data in the current study with a more detailed list of patient factors in terms of specific comorbid conditions or presenting lab and/or imaging findings might potentially be more helpful in targeting preventive interventions, such as vaccination, she said. The study received no outside funding. The researchers and Wasylyshyn had no financial conflicts to disclose. content_title: Health officials see sharp increase of flu and RSV cases in children
content: TEXAS — Chances are, you know someone who is sick or recovering from an illness. Health officials say there’s been a sharp increase in influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) cases in children. Within the state of Texas, there’s been an increase in flu cases, particularly influenza A, according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data and local health officials. The Texas Department of State Health Services started reporting flu cases at the beginning of October, and according to its Respiratory Illness Interactive Dashboard , flu and RSV cases are still high. Texas hospitals and urgent care centers are seeing more children who have the flu every day, but Dr. Natalie Tarrant from Texas Children’s Hospital said we haven’t even seen the peak of flu season yet. “Definitely started earlier than you asked last year. And we don’t know if that means that flu season will just be shifted, where the whole thing starts earlier and ends earlier, or if that means that it’s just going to be a worse year than last year. Last year was worse than the average year for flu,” Tarrant said. But when should you take your child to see a doctor? Dr. Suzanne Whitworth from Cook Children’s Hospital said that, when it comes to children, you have to trust your gut. “Any time you have anxiety and your radar goes off, that you need to see a doctor, call. Either call one or go to urgent care. For sure, you want to go see a doctor if there is any difficulty breathing,” Whitworth said. Dr. Whitworth said a fever can also indicate if your child is very ill. “For healthy, normal children, fever is anything that's a 100.4 or higher rectally. And so if your child has significant fever and they’re not acting right and not feeling okay or dehydrated or not feeling well, that’s another reason to give your doctor a call,” she said. According to Dr. Tarrant, the best way to protect your children from the flu is prevention, and she recommends parents get their children the flu shot. “Vaccination is key. It’s it’s really exciting... as a pediatrician, a new vaccine comes out that changes the landscape of what we see in the office,” Tarrant said. “And the RSV vaccine has been amazing for us. Flu vaccine, we always recommend universally for everybody, but especially the babies, because the babies have a lot of trouble with flu.”
